sentences.text: When no one ever questions those in power, a society can drift into serious trouble.
Some people argue that the well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
I largely agree that questioning authority helps a society, though unlimited questioning can also do harm.
First, questioning authority genuinely strengthens a society.
When people challenge those in power, they help expose corruption and prevent abuse.
For example, citizens who question unjust laws have often pushed societies toward greater fairness.
This shows that healthy questioning keeps leaders honest and accountable.
A society that questions its rulers is far less likely to suffer under tyranny.
Open debate also helps a society find better ideas and correct its mistakes.
To this extent, questioning authority clearly improves a society's well-being.
Second, however, questioning authority without limit can also harm a society.
If people doubt every rule and leader, cooperation and order can break down.
Consider a society where no one trusts the police, the courts, or any shared law.
Such total distrust can lead to chaos rather than to greater well-being.
Some authority, such as fair laws and honest courts, deserves reasonable respect.
Questioning works best when it is thoughtful rather than reckless and endless.
Healthy questioning, then, must be balanced with reasonable trust.
In conclusion, a society benefits greatly when many of its people question authority.
But questioning must have limits, or trust and order may collapse entirely.
A nation thrives when it questions power wisely while still respecting what deserves respect.
